使用 RustStream 的 ZeroMQ Broker ruststream-zeromq 构建 ZeroMQ 服务的指南。
ZeroMQ 如何工作，ruststream-zeromq 在套接字与 RustStream 运行时之间处于什么位置，以及这样做的开销。
订阅读取套接字时，最多领先处理器 read_ahead 条消息；超出就停止读取，等待一直传回对端的发送。
ruststream-zeromq 在每条消息上的开销：与裸 zeromq 客户端对照的吞吐量，以及它自身代码的指令数和内存分配次数。
ruststream-zeromq 如何测量自己：三个循环、用同一进程中的对端代替 Broker、受传输限制的判定计算，以及代码计数。
ruststream-zeromq 的基准测试数字测量的是什么，以及不能从中得出什么结论。
ruststream-zeromq 的位置：在 RustStream 运行时与 zeromq 客户端之间，每个订阅和每个发布者各有一个套接字，没有服务器。
ZmqQueue::new 记录端点，connect 检查它，每个订阅和绑定一端的发布者在启动时接入套接字，拨号连接的发布者在第一次发布时接入。
一条 ZeroMQ 消息穿过 RustStream 服务的路径：套接字任务、通道、处理器、回复的帧和发送。
ack、drop、retry 和 retry_after 在不结算任何东西的 ZeroMQ 上变成什么：ack 回答 Unsupported，重试是服务自己发布的副本。
ZeroMQ 是一个套接字库，套接字之间直接通信：没有服务器，不存储任何东西，由模式决定每条消息由谁接收。
ZMTP 连接以问候和 READY 命令开始，之后承载由帧组成的消息；本 crate 的一条消息是三帧：名称、消息头、载荷。
zeromq 客户端不保存消息队列：一次发送把帧写进对端的连接，在途的数据由内核的套接字缓冲区保存。
The parts of ruststream-zeromq a ZeroMQ service uses, one page per component.
With asyncapi the document says ZeroMQ: protocol zeromq, ZMTP 3.0, and the crate's facts under the x-ruststream-zeromq extension.
A publish channel reports its socket pair and, on PUSH/PULL and PUB/SUB, nameFrame: the frame 0 a peer sends or subscribes with.
A responder's reply channel has no address; the document points a client at $message.header#/reply-to instead.
The server reports the coordinate without scheme or credentials, the transport, the side this service takes and ZMTP 3.0.
Three brokers, one per socket pattern: new records the endpoint with no I/O, and the runtime connects each at startup.
ZmqEndpoint is an address on tcp:// or ipc:// plus the side this process takes; another scheme is refused at connect.
ZmqEndpoint::bind makes this process listen: one subscription reads the bound socket, and port zero lets the system pick.
ZmqEndpoint::connect makes this process dial: dialing subscriptions share a broker, and a broker that only publishes sends as usual.
EndpointRole makes the side a type: ZmqQueue<Connect> dials, the parameter defaults to Bind, and a mount site writes it where it names the type.
ZmqError is the one error type of the crate: endpoint, send, receive, wire, request timeout, not connected, invalid.
Each pattern's prelude offers its policy as Publish; ruststream_zeromq::prelude mounts several patterns under prefixed names.
shutdown closes the connected form at once; a publisher handed out earlier reports ZmqError::NotConnected and never sends.
connect checks the endpoint without I/O; each subscription attaches its socket as it opens, and a refused bind fails the start naming it.
ZmqFanout is PUB/SUB: every subscription whose name prefixes a message gets a copy, and one that attaches late misses what came before.
ZmqQueue is PUSH/PULL: competing consumers, each message reaches one of them, in turn and without a key.
ZmqRpc is DEALER/ROUTER: a responder answers each request at the peer that sent it, on whichever side the endpoint takes.
Each pattern's Publish sends the three frames and nothing else; a send waits up to five seconds for a peer.
A queue publish is cancel-safe; a fan-out publish, a reply and a request are not, so give up through a timeout, not a select! arm.
A queue worker replies through a queue on an endpoint of its own, since the one its subscription binds would hand the reply back to it.
request sends over a DEALER of its own and resolves with the answer matching its correlation-id, or RequestTimeout.
A responder answers at the reply-to address the ROUTER stamps on each request, through a transform that names the destination.
ZeroMQ settles nothing: ack and nack report Unsupported, a plain retry delivers nothing again, and every retry is a copy this service publishes.
dead_letter names where a spent delivery goes; on ZeroMQ that is a publisher on another endpoint, because a name on the own one stays home.
Where copies go follows the side: a bound subscription takes its own, and one that dials and every responder name a destination.
retry_after publishes a copy after the delay, and max_attempts caps the copies through the framework's x-ruststream-retry-count header.
A subscription is a name, and the name is frame 0 of every message; #[subscriber("jobs")] is the whole declaration.
A slice handler on a queue or fan-out gets a batch assembled on this side, closed at the size the mount names or 20 ms after its first delivery.
On ZmqFanout a subscription named orders receives orders.created too: the name is a prefix filter, the protocol's own rule.
read_ahead bounds how many deliveries a subscription reads ahead of its handler, 1000 by default; past it the sender waits.
TestApp::start connects each ZeroMQ broker in process: the pattern's routing, the socket's refusals, and no settlement.
TestApp::start_live runs the same test over loopback sockets in every cargo test, for back-pressure and the real frames.
In the default envelope every message is three frames, name, headers, payload, so a peer in any language composes one with send_multipart.
An envelope is the frame layout of a message: Frames by default, Framed for one codec document, NoOp for the payload alone, or a layout of your own.
The header frame is UTF-8 name: value lines, read when a handler first asks; a header the frame cannot carry is refused on publish.
On DEALER/ROUTER a request carries correlation-id, and its answer travels behind the requester's identity with frame 0 holding reply.

ruststream-zeromq 是 RustStream 的 ZeroMQ Broker，基于纯 Rust 实现的 zeromq 客户端构建。 ZeroMQ 中间没有服务器：服务之间通过 tcp:// 和 ipc:// 套接字直接通信。 本 crate 为每种套接字模式提供一个 Broker。 ZmqQueue 使用 PUSH/PULL 模式，相互竞争的消费者分担工作。 ZmqFanout 使用 PUB/SUB 模式，每个订阅者都收到一份副本。 ZmqRpc 使用 DEALER/ROUTER 模式，传递请求及其回复。 这组指南带着一个 ZeroMQ 服务从安装走到生产环境。 从快速开始读起。
本节用图说明 ZeroMQ 如何工作，ruststream-zeromq 在套接字与 RustStream 运行时之间处于什么位置，以及这给服务带来的开销。

ruststream-zeromq 如何测量自己：三个循环、用同一进程中的对端代替 Broker、受传输限制的判定计算，以及代码计数。流程就是框架自己的流程（RustStream 方法论），本页说明它在 ZeroMQ 上是什么样子。

一个进程把每个场景跑三遍，作为三个循环，它们只有一处不同：承载消息的是什么。 裸客户端。 zeromq 套接字，直接驱动：接收、解码。 Broker crate。 本 crate，上面什么也没有：Broker 建立连接，打开一个订阅，一个循环从它的流中取出消息、解码并 ack。 RustStream。 用户写的服务：一个 #[subscriber] 处理器及其外围的应用。 其余一切在三个循环中都相同：套接字模式、套接字选项、线上的三帧、解码成同一个结构体、载荷字节、tokio 运行时，以及二进制程序。 消息体是 512 字节的 JSON。它解码成一个包含两个整数字段的结构体，因此解码不做内存分配，数字反映的是本 crate，而不是 JSON 解析器。

框架的其他每个 Broker crate 都拿自己和一台服务器对照：启动一个容器，客户端连接它，这一行就是该 crate 在这个客户端之上增加的开销。ZeroMQ 的对端彼此直接通信。每个循环的另一端都是同一进程里的一个 PUSH 套接字，使用默认的套接字选项，运行时除了二进制本身不启动任何东西。 路径上没有服务器的传输，每条消息的开销很低。于是本 crate 自己的工作在总开销中所占的份额比在其他任何地方都大，同样的开销在这里读出的百分比，比对照 Broker 时更大。

每次运行使用新地址，环回地址上的新端口或新的 ipc:// 路径，因此一次运行永远遇不到之前的运行留下的连接。 在三个循环中，计时窗口都从第一条消息开始，到最后一条消息解码完成时结束。 绑定和握手都在窗口之外。 消息条数来自一次探测，它测量裸循环的速率，因此在任何机器上，测量的运行都至少持续五秒。 各循环交替进行：裸、crate、RustStream，共三轮。每个循环报告它最佳、中位和最差的一轮。 当一条消息的大部分时间都在等待传输，因而上层的工作发生在已经付出的等待之内时，该行标为 受传输限制。这是算出来的：同一传输上一次交换的往返时间，乘以一条消息花费的往返次数，再与测得的每条消息的时间相比。往返时间在所有循环之外用一对 REQ/REP 测量，并与机器信息一起公布。PUSH/PULL 消费者不回发任何东西，因此一条消息花费零次往返，没有任何一行受传输限制。

开销图的每个场景都是用户写的服务，基于生产 Broker，绑定到环回地址上的一个 TCP 端口，构建时不带 testing 特性。对端是一个裸 zeromq 套接字，运行在自己的线程上，写出本 crate 的三帧。 对端在计数开始之前、服务还没有读取时写出全部消息，消息在内核的缓冲区里等待。PUSH/PULL 会为尚未读取的消费者保留它们，因此消费场景和批场景使用它。应答场景是 DEALER/ROUTER，回答发回提出请求的对端，它的计数一直持续到对端读完所有回答。 指令数来自 callgrind，内存分配来自 DHAT。一个场景依次在一条消息、1000 条、2000 条上运行。后两次之差是一条消息的稳态开销，单条消息就是冷启动。 同一个二进制程序运行三次，消费场景的指令数完全相同，另外两个场景相差在千分之三以内：对端如何读取回答、批何时结束，取决于时序。内存分配次数相差在一个块以内。与保存的基线对照时，某个场景的指令数多出百分之二就算失败。内存分配在每次运行中都受每个场景声明的下限约束。

just bench 该命令运行两个对照场景，并重写 docs/benchmarks/results.json。它不启动任何测试环境，因为对端是同一进程里的套接字。它需要几分钟，并要求独占机器。它会清空 RUSTFLAGS，因此二进制程序不绑定于构建它的 CPU。两个命令都按发布构建的方式构建基准测试，在各 crate 之间使用完整的链接时优化（fat LTO），因此数字描述的是服务实际发布的代码。 just bench-code 代码计数只需几秒，需要 valgrind。该命令自己安装基准测试运行器，版本为发布版 Cargo.lock 固定的版本。在 main 上运行 just bench-code --save-baseline=main 记录基线，在分支上运行 just bench-code --baseline=main 与之对照。just bench-code 2000 让每个场景在两千条消息上计数，而不是一千条。

The parts of ruststream-zeromq a ZeroMQ service uses, one page per component. The brokers come first: ZmqQueue, ZmqFanout and ZmqRpc, the ZmqEndpoint each binds or connects, their startup, shutdown, preludes and errors. Subscriptions follow, with their prefixes, batches and read-ahead. Acknowledgement covers what a delivery settles on ZeroMQ, retries and dead letters. Publishing covers the publish policies, replies and cancellation, and Request-reply the requester and the responder. Wire format shows the frames a peer in another language sends, AsyncAPI what the generated document reports, and Testing the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on.

With the asyncapi feature the document says ZeroMQ: protocol zeromq, ZMTP 3.0, and the crate's facts under the x-ruststream-zeromq extension. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. The specification has no ZeroMQ binding, and its binding keys are a closed list. So this crate reports everything it knows in one extension, x-ruststream-zeromq, at two levels. A server says how to attach to the endpoint: the transport, the coordinate and the side this service takes. A channel says which socket pair its messages travel over and what their name frame holds. A responder's reply channel has no address, and the operation points a client at the reply address instead. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the brokers, their endpoints and the destinations the mount sites resolved. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen. Peers in other languages reads from the document how a peer joins each channel.

The dependency line: ruststream-zeromq = { version = "0.8", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers each broker under a label, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example zmq_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled("jobs", jobs(), |b| { b.include(work).out_reply(ZmqQueuePublish) }) .with_broker_labeled("rpc", greeter(), |b| { b.include(greet) .out_reply(ZmqRpcPublish) .transform(ReplyToRequester) .out_retry(ZmqRpcPublish) .to("greeter.retry") }) } examples/manual/zmq_asyncapi.rs fn app() -> impl App { // Each label is the key of the broker's server in the document. A publish channel reports its socket pair and, on PUSH/PULL and PUB/SUB, nameFrame: the frame 0 a peer sends or subscribes with. Each destination a mount site publishes to is a channel of the document. Its x-ruststream-zeromq extension comes from the publish policy, so it says how messages leave this service. socketPair is PUSH/PULL, PUB/SUB or DEALER/ROUTER. nameFrame is the value frame 0 holds on the wire, which is the destination itself. A peer reads from it what to send to reach the channel and, on PUB/SUB, which prefix to subscribe with. A responder's reply channel reports no nameFrame. An answer travels to the identity the ROUTER supplies, and its frame 0 always holds reply, so the channel's own name reaches no peer. Peers in other languages shows which frame 0 a peer sends or subscribes with.

The worker's results go to results over PUSH/PULL, so the channel reports nameFrame: results. Macros Manual examples/zmq_asyncapi.rs // No destination of its own: the clause names `results`, the name frame of every result. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Done { id: u64, } #[subscriber("jobs", reply("results"))] async fn work(job: &Job) -> Done { tracing::info!(job.id, "working"); Done { id: job.id } } examples/manual/zmq_asyncapi.rs #[derive(Debug, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Done { id: u64, } // No destination of its own: the mount names `results`, the name frame of every result. impl OutgoingDestination for Done { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Done { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Work; impl Handle<Job, Done> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Done, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "working"); ready(Ok(Done { id: job.id })) } }

A responder's reply channel has no address; the document points a client at $message.header#/reply-to instead. A responder answers each request at the peer that sent it, so no fixed name addresses its answers. When the reply position carries a transform that names the destination, as a responder does, the document reports the reply channel with address: null. The receive operation's reply.address.location is $message.header#/reply-to, the header the ROUTER stamps on each request. The channel keeps the fallback name from reply("..") as its key. Peers in other languages asks such a responder from a Python DEALER.

The greeter's answer names no destination, and a transform names it per request. The mount on the AsyncAPI page puts the transform on the reply position. Macros Manual examples/zmq_asyncapi.rs // The ROUTER addresses each answer per request, so `reply` is only the fallback name. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Answer { text: String, } #[subscriber("greeter", reply("reply"))] async fn greet(request: &Greeting) -> Answer { Answer { text: format!("hello {}", request.who), } } /// Answers at the `reply-to` address the ROUTER stamped on the request, under the request's /// `correlation-id`. #[derive(Clone)] struct ReplyToRequester; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ReplyToRequester { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(reply_to) = cx.headers().get_shared("reply-to") && let Ok(reply_to) = Str::try_from(reply_to) { out.set_name(reply_to); } if let Some(correlation) = cx.headers().get_shared("correlation-id") { out.headers_mut() .insert(Str::from_static("correlation-id"), correlation); } } } examples/manual/zmq_asyncapi.rs #[derive(Debug, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Answer { text: String, } // The ROUTER addresses each answer per request, so `reply` is only the fallback name. impl OutgoingDestination for Answer { type Form = CallerName; The server reports the coordinate without scheme or credentials, the transport, the side this service takes and ZMTP 3.0. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the endpoint's address without the scheme, such as 0.0.0.0:5557; an ipc:// endpoint reports its socket path whole. User information in the address stays out of it, because the document is published and shared. The protocol is zeromq, and protocolVersion is 3.0, the ZMTP version the client greets every peer with. The x-ruststream-zeromq extension of the server holds three fields. transport is tcp or ipc. endpoint is the same coordinate as host. role is bind when this service listens on the endpoint and connect when it dials it, so a peer reads which side it takes. Peers in other languages reads the address and the side of each server from the document.

The worker dials the dispatcher at worker:5555, and the greeter listens on every interface at port 5557. The document reports the first as role: connect and the second as role: bind. Macros Manual examples/zmq_asyncapi.rs /// The worker dials the dispatcher that hands out the jobs. fn jobs() -> ZmqQueue<Connect> { ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://worker:5555")) } /// The greeter listens on every interface. fn greeter() -> ZmqRpc { ZmqRpc::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5557")) } examples/manual/zmq_asyncapi.rs /// The worker dials the dispatcher that hands out the jobs. fn jobs() -> ZmqQueue<Connect> { ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://worker:5555")) } /// The greeter listens on every interface. fn greeter() -> ZmqRpc { ZmqRpc::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5557")) }

Three brokers, one per socket pattern: new records the endpoint with no I/O, and the runtime connects each at startup. ZeroMQ has no server in the middle. Two processes talk directly, over a socket pair the pattern names. The pattern decides who receives a message, and the endpoint decides which side listens. Broker Sockets Who receives a message Publish policy ZmqQueue PUSH/PULL one of the competing consumers, in turn ZmqQueuePublish ZmqFanout PUB/SUB every subscription whose name is a prefix of the message's ZmqFanoutPublish ZmqRpc DEALER/ROUTER the responder, and its answer the peer that asked ZmqRpcPublish Each broker's new takes a ZmqEndpoint and opens nothing, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. At startup the runtime connects it and receives its connected form, such as ConnectedZmqQueue. The connect checks the endpoint's scheme and opens no socket: each subscription and each publisher attaches its own socket when it first opens, as Startup describes. At shutdown the runtime consumes the connected form, and a publisher handed out earlier reports an error from then on, as Shutdown describes. Each pattern's publish policy is also the default of its connected form. So a reply handler mounted with no publish position answers through its own pattern. Each pattern's prelude offers its policy as Publish, so moving a service to another pattern changes its import line and leaves the mount site as it is. Getting started runs a first worker on a queue and feeds it from a Python peer.

A worker stage of a pipeline binds tcp://0.0.0.0:5555, and any peer that pushes the three frames feeds it. cargo run --example zmq_pipeline --features testing -- run starts it. Macros Manual examples/zmq_pipeline.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; #[subscriber("jobs")] async fn handle(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "working on the job"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/zmq_pipeline.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| b.include(handle), ) } examples/manual/zmq_pipeline.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; struct Work; impl Handle<Job> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "working on the job"); ready(Ok(())) } } examples/manual/zmq_pipeline.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()), ) }

ZmqEndpoint is an address on tcp:// or ipc:// plus the side this process takes; another scheme is refused at connect. Two constructors fix the side. ZmqEndpoint::bind makes this process listen, and ZmqEndpoint::connect makes it dial. The side is part of the type, and the broker built on the endpoint carries it, as EndpointRole describes. tcp://host:port reaches another host. ipc:///path is a socket file on the same host, with no network stack in between. When the broker connects, an address with any other scheme fails startup with ZmqError::Invalid, naming the address, before any socket opens. address returns the address as written. The endpoint and its side are the whole configuration of a broker. The ZeroMQ implementation carries no CURVE or ZAP layer, so traffic is neither authenticated nor encrypted: a service runs on a trusted network or inside a tunnel. Running in production reads the endpoints from the environment.

A worker listens on a socket file for the producers on its host, and pushes its results to a collector it dials over the network. Macros Manual examples/zmq_broker_endpoint.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // This process dials the collector, which listens on another host. let collector = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://collector:5560")).bindable(); let results = collector.bind(Publish); // This process listens, on a socket file the producers of this host dial. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("ipc:///tmp/jobs")), |b| { b.include(work).out_reply(results) }) .register_broker(collector) } examples/manual/zmq_broker_endpoint.rs fn app() -> impl App { // This process dials the collector, which listens on another host. let collector = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://collector:5560")).bindable(); let results = collector.bind(Publish); // This process listens, on a socket file the producers of this host dial. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("ipc:///tmp/jobs")), |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).reply().build()) .out_reply(results) }) .register_broker(collector) }

ZmqEndpoint::bind makes this process listen: one subscription reads the bound socket, and port zero lets the system pick. A bound endpoint is one listening socket, and it belongs to the subscription that bound it. A second subscription on the same broker fails startup with an error that names both subscriptions. So two kinds of work take two brokers, each on an endpoint of its own. When the subscription closes, the endpoint is free for the next one. The subscription binds its socket as it opens, and a port another process holds fails startup, as Startup describes. With port zero, as in tcp://127.0.0.1:0, the system picks the port when the subscription binds. A publisher of the same service dials the port the system picked, so a service that holds both ends runs with no fixed port. A broker that binds an endpoint and has no subscription on it listens through its publisher from the moment the service starts, and the peers dial it before its first publish. When a subscription of the same broker binds the endpoint later, the publisher gives the endpoint up first, on a fixed port and on port zero alike, and its next publish dials that subscription. So a handler that publishes into a queue whose subscription opens after its own reaches that subscription once it is open. On a bound endpoint that a subscription of this service reads, a ZmqQueue publisher sends only under the subscription's own name. Pipelines with PUSH/PULL decides which side of a pipeline binds.

A worker listens for jobs on one endpoint and for reports on another. Each broker is labeled, so a test addresses it by name. Macros Manual examples/zmq_broker_bind.rs /// The service on the two addresses it listens on, one per subscription. fn service(jobs: &str, reports: &str) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled("jobs", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(jobs)), |b| { b.include(work) }) .with_broker_labeled("reports", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(reports)), |b| { b.include(file_report) }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555", "tcp://0.0.0.0:5556") } examples/manual/zmq_broker_bind.rs /// The service on the two addresses it listens on, one per subscription. fn service(jobs: &str, reports: &str) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled("jobs", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(jobs)), |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) }) .with_broker_labeled("reports", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(reports)), |b| { b.include(subscriber("reports", FileReport).build()) }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555", "tcp://0.0.0.0:5556") }

ZmqEndpoint::connect makes this process dial: dialing subscriptions share a broker, and a broker that only publishes sends as usual. Each subscription that dials is a socket of its own on the peer's endpoint. So one broker takes several of them: two ZmqQueue workers dialing one ventilator split its stream, and two ZmqFanout watchers dialing one publisher each receive their own prefix. A subscription that dials reads from the sending end of its pattern, a ventilator's PUSH socket or a publisher's PUB socket, and that peer takes nothing. So once a subscription of this service has dialed the endpoint, a publish through the same ZmqQueue or ZmqFanout is refused with ZmqError::Send, naming the subscription. For the same reason a dialing subscription's retry copies go where its mount site names. A broker that only publishes, such as a worker's link to the sink that collects its results, dials and sends as usual. Pipelines with PUSH/PULL runs workers that dial both the ventilator and the sink.

A pipeline worker dials both ends: the ventilator it pulls jobs from and the sink it pushes results to. Every copy of the worker runs the same app, so the service scales by starting more of them. The results and the retry copies of failed jobs leave for the sink. Macros Manual examples/zmq_broker_connect.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; #[subscriber("jobs", reply)] async fn work(job: &Job) -> Done { tracing::info!(job.id, "working on the job"); Done { id: job.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The sink listens; this worker dials it and only publishes there. let sink = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://sink:5556")).bindable(); let results = sink.bind(Publish); let failed = sink.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled( "ventilator", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://ventilator:5555")), |b| { // The ventilator only pushes: results and retry copies leave for the sink. b.include(work) .out_reply(results) .out_retry(failed) .to("jobs.failed") }, ) .with_broker_labeled("sink", sink, |b| b) } examples/manual/zmq_broker_connect.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; struct Work; impl Handle<Job, Done> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Done, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "working on the job"); ready(Ok(Done { id: job.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The sink listens; this worker dials it and only publishes there. let sink = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://sink:5556")).bindable(); let results = sink.bind(Publish); let failed = sink.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled( "ventilator", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://ventilator:5555")), |b| { // The ventilator only pushes: results and retry copies leave for the sink. b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).reply().build()) .out_reply(results) .out_retry(failed) .to("jobs.failed") }, ) .with_broker_labeled("sink", sink, |b| b) }

EndpointRole makes the side a type: ZmqQueue<Connect> dials, the parameter defaults to Bind, and a mount site writes it where it names the type. ZmqEndpoint::bind returns a ZmqEndpoint<Bind>, and ZmqEndpoint::connect returns a ZmqEndpoint<Connect>. ZmqQueue and ZmqFanout carry the same Bind or Connect as their Role parameter, so ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect(..)) is a ZmqQueue<Connect>. The parameter defaults to Bind, so ZmqQueue alone names a queue this process binds. ZmqRpc has no Role parameter. A mount site writes the side only where it names the type: a Router for a queue it dials is a Router<ZmqQueue<Connect>>, and a test addresses that broker as tb.broker::<ZmqQueue<Connect>>(). The side decides where a retry copy can go, and the compiler holds a routes file to it. On ZmqQueue<Connect>, a router chain whose out_retry names no destination does not compile. EndpointRole is the bound a helper writes to build a broker on either side. The trait is sealed: Bind and Connect are the whole set.

A worker's routes on the queue it dials send their retry copies to a queue the worker binds. One helper builds both queues with the same read-ahead, whichever side the endpoint takes. Macros Manual examples/zmq_broker_role.rs /// The worker's routes on a queue it dials: the copies go to the queue `copies` publishes to. fn routes(copies: Bound<ZmqQueue, Publish>) -> impl RouterDef<ZmqQueue<Connect>> { Router::<ZmqQueue<Connect>>::new() .include(work) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .out_retry(copies) .to("jobs") .build() } /// One queue setting for both sides of an endpoint. fn queue<Role: EndpointRole>(endpoint: ZmqEndpoint<Role>) -> ZmqQueue<Role> { ZmqQueue::new(endpoint).read_ahead(nonzero!(64_usize)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let retries = queue(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5560")).bindable(); let copies = retries.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(queue(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://ventilator:5555")), |b| { b.include_router(routes(copies)) }) .with_broker(retries, |b| b.include(work).max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32))) } examples/manual/zmq_broker_role.rs /// The worker's routes on a queue it dials: the copies go to the queue `copies` publishes to. fn routes(copies: Bound<ZmqQueue, Publish>) -> impl RouterDef<ZmqQueue<Connect>> { Router::<ZmqQueue<Connect>>::new() .include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .out_retry(copies) .to("jobs") .build() } /// One queue setting for both sides of an endpoint. fn queue<Role: EndpointRole>(endpoint: ZmqEndpoint<Role>) -> ZmqQueue<Role> { ZmqQueue::new(endpoint).read_ahead(nonzero!(64_usize)) } fn app() -> impl App { let retries = queue(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5560")).bindable(); let copies = retries.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(queue(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://ventilator:5555")), |b| { b.include_router(routes(copies)) }) .with_broker(retries, |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) }) }

ZmqError is the one error type of the crate: endpoint, send, receive, wire, request timeout, not connected, invalid. Each variant names the step that failed. The ZeroMQ client's own error is the source of Endpoint, so the client's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Endpoint a socket could not bind or dial its address, such as a port another process holds at startup, or a peer that did not listen within 30 seconds Send a message could not leave: a publish its own subscription would receive back, a publish to a peer that only sends, an answer to a requester that has gone, a header the text frame cannot carry, or no peer within five seconds Receive an open subscription failed to receive Wire a peer sent frames that do not follow the wire layout RequestTimeout a request got no answer within its timeout NotConnected a publisher, a responder or a request was used after the broker shut down Invalid an address with a scheme other than tcp:// or ipc://, or a second subscription on an endpoint the broker binds A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, with the unsent message whenever the socket never took it, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. A publish the runtime makes for a handler (a reply, a retry copy, a dead letter) that fails reaches the handler's .error(..) continuation instead. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

A result the socket refuses is logged with its cause, and the job is settled as a retry in a second. Macros Manual examples/zmq_broker_errors.rs #[subscriber("jobs")] async fn work(job: &Job, Out(results): Out<impl Publisher, Results>) -> HandlerOutcome { if let Err(err) = results.message(&Done { id: job.id }).publish().await { // The error names the destination and the socket's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "jobs", job.id, error = %err, "result not published"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(1)); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/zmq_broker_errors.rs struct Work; impl<Entry> Handle<Job, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Work where Entry: OutEntry<Results, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let done = Done { id: job.id }; if let Err(err) = outs.get(Results).message(&done).publish().await { // The error names the destination and the socket's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "jobs", job.id, error = %err, "result not published"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(1))); } Ok(()) } }

Each pattern's prelude offers its policy as Publish; ruststream_zeromq::prelude mounts several patterns under prefixed names. A routes file on one pattern imports that pattern's prelude: queue::prelude, fanout::prelude or rpc::prelude. Each carries the core's prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. Each adds ZmqEndpoint, the pattern's broker and its publish policy under the name every broker crate uses, Publish. rpc::prelude also brings RequestReply, the capability only ZmqRpc implements. So moving a service to another pattern changes the import line, and the mount site stays as it is. A file that mounts more than one pattern imports ruststream_zeromq::prelude. One glob cannot carry three policies under one name, so this prelude names them ZmqQueuePublish, ZmqFanoutPublish and ZmqRpcPublish. It also carries the three brokers, RequestReply and the modules queue, fanout and rpc. A handler body bounds its injected publisher with a core capability, such as Out<impl Publisher, Slot>, and imports ruststream::prelude::* alone. A ZeroMQ send takes the frames alone, so a handler body stays on the core's prelude, whichever pattern it runs on. Broadcast with PUB/SUB mounts a queue and a fan-out in one file with the crate's prelude.

A worker takes jobs from a queue and announces each finished job on a fan-out, so the routes file imports the crate's prelude. Macros Manual examples/zmq_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_zeromq::prelude::*; #[subscriber("jobs", reply)] async fn work(job: &Job) -> Done { tracing::info!(job.id, "working on the job"); Done { id: job.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // Every listener that dials the fan-out hears about each finished job. let events = ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5556")).bindable(); let announce = events.bind(ZmqFanoutPublish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| b.include(work).out_reply(announce), ) .register_broker(events) } examples/manual/zmq_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_zeromq::prelude::*; struct Work; impl Handle<Job, Done> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Done, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "working on the job"); ready(Ok(Done { id: job.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { // Every listener that dials the fan-out hears about each finished job. let events = ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5556")).bindable(); let announce = events.bind(ZmqFanoutPublish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).reply().build()) .out_reply(announce) }, ) .register_broker(events) }

shutdown closes the connected form at once; a publisher handed out earlier reports ZmqError::NotConnected and never sends. The crate keeps no queue of its own, so the broker has nothing to flush and its shutdown returns at once. The runtime first stops the subscriptions and lets the handlers in flight finish. Then it shuts each broker down, and a subscription's socket closes as the runtime drops it. A publisher can outlive the broker: one a startup hook kept, one a sibling task took from RunningApp::publisher, or a clone of either. After shutdown, a publish through it returns ZmqError::NotConnected with the message it did not send. An answer and a request after shutdown fail the same way. Running in production covers what a service does at shutdown.

The service announces on a fan-out that it has started. The hook's publisher lives as long as the hook; a task that kept it past shutdown would get ZmqError::NotConnected from its next publish. Macros Manual examples/zmq_broker_shutdown.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5557")), |b| { // The publisher lives as long as the hook; a task that kept it past shutdown would // get `ZmqError::NotConnected` from it. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "worker".to_owned(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }) }, ) } examples/manual/zmq_broker_shutdown.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5557")), |b| { // The publisher lives as long as the hook; a task that kept it past shutdown would // get `ZmqError::NotConnected` from it. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "worker".to_owned(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }) }, ) }

connect checks the endpoint without I/O; each subscription attaches its socket as it opens, and a refused bind fails the start naming it. When the runtime connects a broker, the connect checks the endpoint's scheme and opens nothing. An address that is neither tcp:// nor ipc:// fails startup with ZmqError::Invalid, naming the address. Each subscription opens its own socket as the runtime opens the subscription. A subscription on a bound endpoint binds it, and a port another process holds fails startup with ZmqError::Endpoint, naming the address. A subscription that dials waits for its peer to listen. The ZeroMQ client retries the connection for up to 30 seconds, then the start fails with ZmqError::Endpoint, naming the address. A publisher on the bind side attaches its socket at startup, so it listens before its first publish; a publisher that dials attaches on its first publish, the same way. The sockets attach, and their drivers run, on the runtime the broker connected on. So a handler that runs on threads of its own, mounted with threads(n), publishes through the same sockets as every other handler. Running in production covers the order in which services start.

The worker binds the address service takes, and opens it when the runtime starts the subscription. A test starts the same service on an address that fails, to see the error the service would stop with. Macros Manual examples/zmq_broker_startup.rs /// The worker on the address `jobs` names; nothing is opened until the runtime starts it. fn service(jobs: &str) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(jobs)), |b| b.include(work)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555") } examples/manual/zmq_broker_startup.rs /// The worker on the address `jobs` names; nothing is opened until the runtime starts it. fn service(jobs: &str) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(jobs)), |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) }) } fn app() -> impl App { service("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555") }

ZmqFanout is PUB/SUB: every subscription whose name prefixes a message gets a copy, and one that attaches late misses what came before. The subscription's name is its filter, and the filter is a prefix, the protocol's own rule. #[subscriber("orders")] receives orders.created and orders.shipped, and never payments.settled; the prefixes page covers the rule. A message that matches no subscription is dropped, and the publisher gets no error. Nothing is stored. A subscription that attaches after a publisher has started misses what that publisher sent before it arrived. This is the slow joiner of ZeroMQ. A publisher that reaches a subscription of its own service reads that subscription's filter before its first send, so inside one service nothing is lost to it. The policy is ZmqFanoutPublish, offered as Publish by fanout::prelude. A PUB socket is held back by its slowest matching subscriber, as read_ahead describes. A retry copy on a fan-out the subscription binds goes back to that subscription's listener and reaches the audience the original had. A subscription that dials reads from a publisher that takes nothing back, so its mount site names where the copies go, as on ZmqQueue. Broadcast with PUB/SUB announces finished jobs to watchers that subscribe by prefix.

An auditor binds a fan-out, and the order services dial it. Its subscription on orders receives every order event, whatever comes after the prefix. Macros Manual examples/zmq_broker_fanout.rs use ruststream_zeromq::fanout::prelude::*; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn audit(event: &OrderEvent) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.order_id, "order event audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The order services dial this endpoint and publish `orders.created`, `orders.shipped`, ... RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("auditor", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5556")), |b| b.include(audit), ) } examples/manual/zmq_broker_fanout.rs use ruststream_zeromq::fanout::prelude::*; struct Audit; impl Handle<OrderEvent> for Audit { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.order_id, "order event audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The order services dial this endpoint and publish `orders.created`, `orders.shipped`, ... RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("auditor", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5556")), |b| b.include(subscriber("orders", Audit).build()), ) }

ZmqQueue is PUSH/PULL: competing consumers, each message reaches one of them, in turn and without a key. A pipeline has a ventilator that pushes work, workers that pull it, and a sink that collects the results. Workers that dial one ventilator compete for its stream: each message reaches one of them, and none reaches two. PUSH hands the messages out in turn across the attached peers, whatever a message holds. Order holds per socket pair and nowhere else. A subscription that binds its endpoint takes every message a peer pushes into it, whatever the name in frame 0 says. So a second kind of work takes an endpoint of its own. The policy is ZmqQueuePublish, offered as Publish by queue::prelude. A publish to an endpoint that a subscription of this service binds reaches that subscription and nothing else. A message under the subscription's own name goes through: a retry copy, or a job the service feeds itself. A message under any other name is refused with ZmqError::Send, naming it and the subscription, because the subscription would receive it as its next job. So results and replies leave through a queue on an endpoint of its own, as the replies page shows. A retry copy is a message this service publishes. On a bound queue the copy goes back into the queue, and whichever worker is free takes it. A queue that dials reads from a ventilator that takes nothing back, so its mount site names where the copies go; out_retry covers both forms. Pipelines with PUSH/PULL builds a ventilator, competing workers and a sink on it.

Two workers dial one ventilator, and each job it pushes reaches one of them. Their retry copies go to a queue this service binds, where the same handler takes them. ZmqRpc is DEALER/ROUTER: a responder answers each request at the peer that sent it, on whichever side the endpoint takes. A responder is a subscription on a ROUTER socket. The ROUTER stamps each request with a reply-to header that addresses the peer that sent it. A publish transform sets the answer's destination to that address, so the reply type declares no destination of its own, and the name in reply("..") is the fallback the AsyncAPI document reports. The responders page shows the transform. An answer whose requester has gone is refused with ZmqError::Send, naming the reply address. ZmqRpc carries no side in its type: ZmqRpc::new takes an endpoint that binds or one that dials. One policy, ZmqRpcPublish, serves both directions. It routes answers through the responder's ROUTER, and it sends requests over a DEALER socket of its own through the RequestReply capability. rpc::prelude offers it as Publish, together with RequestReply. A responder answers each request at its own address, so .batch(..) on a responder does not compile. A copy of a request has no address of its own, so a responder subscription addresses no retry copies. Every responder mount names where they go, with .out_retry(policy).to(".."), and a mount that names nothing fails startup with an error that names the subscription. A plain name reaches no peer on DEALER/ROUTER. A service that wants the copies to arrive sends them through a queue on another broker; a service that does not names a destination to say so and lets the requester ask again. Request and reply builds a scoring responder and a checkout service that asks it.

A greeter binds tcp://0.0.0.0:5557 and answers each request at the peer that asked. Its retry copies go to greeter.retry, a name that reaches no peer: a requester that gets no answer asks again. Each pattern's Publish sends the three frames and nothing else; a send waits up to five seconds for a peer. Each pattern ships one publish policy: ZmqQueuePublish, ZmqFanoutPublish and ZmqRpcPublish. The pattern's prelude offers it as Publish, and the crate prelude offers all three under their own names. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish).build() for a slot, .out_retry(Publish) for retry copies. The policy holds no connection. At startup the runtime pairs it with the connected broker into a live publisher, such as ZmqQueuePublisher. To publish through another broker of the service, the mount site binds the policy to it with bindable() and .bind(Publish). Pipelines with PUSH/PULL publishes a worker's results to a sink this way. A publish sends the message in its envelope, by default the three frames: its name, its headers and the payload the codec wrote. The payload frame is the buffer the codec wrote, so a payload of any size is sent without a copy. A ZMTP send takes the frames and nothing else, so every publisher declares Options = (), and the publish builder carries the core's steps alone. A handler body therefore imports ruststream::prelude::* alone and bounds its publisher with the capability it needs. A publisher on the bind side attaches its socket when the service starts, so a peer that dials it connects before the first message. A publisher that dials attaches on its first publish and waits for a peer. When no peer has completed the handshake within five seconds, the publish fails with ZmqError::Send, "no connected peer", and the error carries the message back whole. The window is a constant of the crate. Who receives the message is the pattern's rule. On ZmqQueue one peer takes it, in turn. On ZmqFanout every subscriber whose filter is a prefix of the name takes a copy, and a message no subscriber matches is dropped without an error. On ZmqRpc the publisher sends replies only, and a request goes through request. A publish is one send of one message, and a queue publish is safe to cancel, as Cancellation describes.

A queue publish is cancel-safe; a fan-out publish, a reply and a request are not, so give up through a timeout, not a select! arm. A publish waits while the peer applies back-pressure, so a caller may drop it before it completes. On ZmqQueue that is safe. A publish dropped before the socket took its message sends nothing. One dropped in the middle of the send leaves its message with the publisher, and the next publish through it completes that send before its own. A fan-out publish and a reply are not cancel-safe. Dropping one can leave the message half handed to the socket. On a reply, the requester then waits out its timeout. Dropping a request closes the DEALER socket it went out on: an answer already on its way is lost, and the request itself may have reached the responder. So a handler gives up on a request through its timeout, which ends the wait cleanly and returns ZmqError::RequestTimeout. A fan-out publish or a reply that must not hold up other work runs in a task of its own rather than inside a select! arm. Request and reply gives up on a request through its timeout and asks again later.

The handler asks the pricing service for a quote and waits at most two seconds. With no quote in time it settles the order as a retry in thirty seconds. A queue worker replies through a queue on an endpoint of its own, since the one its subscription binds would hand the reply back to it. A reply type that owns its destination names it with #[outgoing(name = "..")], and the subscriber clause stays a bare reply. A type that names nothing takes the name the clause gives, #[subscriber("jobs", reply("results"))]. The generated document reports the destination either form resolves to. A queue that a subscription of this service binds takes every message pushed into it, whatever its name frame says. A reply published there would come back to the same handler as its next job. So the publisher refuses it with ZmqError::Send, naming the destination, and the in-process test broker refuses it the same way. The worker sends its replies through a second broker instead: an endpoint the sink binds, which the worker dials. bindable() turns that broker into a token, .bind(Publish) makes the reply policy publish through it, and register_broker adds it to the service. On ZmqFanout a reply on the fan-out the subscription reads reaches every subscription of the service whose name is a prefix of the reply's name, its own included when it matches. On ZmqRpc a reply goes back to the peer that asked, as Responders shows. Pipelines with PUSH/PULL sends a worker's results to the sink this way.

request sends over a DEALER of its own and resolves with the answer matching its correlation-id, or RequestTimeout. ZmqRpcPublisher implements the core's RequestReply capability, and it is the only publisher of the crate that does. A handler bounds its slot Out<impl RequestReply>, and the mount site binds ZmqRpcPublish to it. request(message, timeout) takes an OutgoingMessage of bytes the handler encoded, and its name is the name frame of the request. The request goes to the broker directly, past the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers. Each request opens a DEALER socket of its own and dials the broker's endpoint, with the frames Identity frame shows. The dial waits as long as the timeout allows, ten seconds at most, and a failed dial returns ZmqError::Endpoint. The request carries a correlation-id header: the one the caller set, or a fresh one. The DEALER keeps reading until an answer carries the same id, and the call returns that answer as a ZmqMessage, which the handler decodes. With no matching answer within the timeout, the call returns ZmqError::RequestTimeout. The responder on the other side copies the id onto its answer. The timeout is the way to give up on a request: dropping the call closes its DEALER, as Cancellation describes. After shutdown a request returns ZmqError::NotConnected. Request and reply asks a scoring service about each order from inside a handler.

A responder answers at the reply-to address the ROUTER stamps on each request, through a transform that names the destination. A responder is an ordinary reply handler on a ZmqRpc subscription. Its ROUTER socket reads the identity of the peer behind each request and stamps the request with a reply-to header that addresses that peer, zmq-reply: and the identity in hex. The reply publisher routes an answer to such an address only. It refuses any other name with ZmqError::Send, so an answer that misses its address fails where it is sent. A publish transform on the reply position sets the destination per request. It reads the delivery being answered, so it implements PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options>, and it names the destination, so it declares Destination = Names. It copies reply-to into the destination and correlation-id into the answer's headers, so the requester matches the answer to its request. get_shared hands each header over as the buffer the request arrived in, so answering costs a reference count rather than a copy. The answer type derives Outgoing without a name: a position offers the naming right only where the type declares no destination. The name in reply("reply") is the fallback that the document reports. An answer whose requester has gone is refused with ZmqError::Send, naming the reply address: the ROUTER holds no peer under that identity. A responder addresses no retry copies of its own, so every responder mount names where they go with .out_retry(Publish).to(".."). Request and reply builds a scoring responder with this transform.

ZeroMQ settles nothing: ack and nack report Unsupported, a plain retry delivers nothing again, and every retry is a copy this service publishes. ZMTP has no frame that settles a delivery. A message reaches the subscription once, and the socket keeps no copy of it. So ack and nack on a delivery report AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs a warning naming the subscription. An ack and a drop both end the delivery, and nothing comes back after either. A retry asks the transport to deliver the message again, and the transport has nothing to deliver: the handler is not called again. A retry_after(delay) is served by the runtime instead. It publishes a copy of the delivery once the delay is over, and the copy arrives as a new message, as Retries describes. Under a cap a plain retry travels as such a copy too. Where the copies go follows the side of the endpoint, as out_retry describes. A delivery reports no redelivery_count: the framework counts its copies in a header of its own. Delivery is at most once, as Settlement draws. A process that stops loses what its subscriptions had read and not yet handled, and every copy still waiting out its delay. Retries and dead letters retries jobs and parks failed invoices on a transport that delivers at most once.

A payment of nothing is dropped. A payment the gateway fails comes back as a copy 10 seconds later, through the queue the service binds. Macros Manual examples/zmq_settlement_at_most_once.rs #[subscriber("payments")] async fn charge(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.amount == 0 { // Nothing to charge. dead_letter(name) names where a spent delivery goes; on ZeroMQ that is a publisher on another endpoint, because a name on the own one stays home. When a retry would go past the cap of max_attempts, the runtime publishes the delivery under the dead-letter name instead, payload and headers as they arrived. A mount with a dead-letter name and no cap sends every failed delivery there at once. A cap with no dead-letter name drops the spent delivery with a warning naming the subscription. A name is frame 0, not an address, and the dead letter leaves through the retry publisher. On the subscription's own bound queue that publisher refuses jobs.dead with ZmqError::Send, and the delivery is dropped with a warning. On the subscription's own bound fan-out jobs.dead matches the prefix jobs and comes back to the subscription that gave up on it. So a dead letter leaves through a publisher on another endpoint, set with .out_retry(..). The retry copies leave through that publisher as well, so such a mount sends every failed delivery to the dead letters, with no retry first. A handler that should see its retries again keeps .out_retry(..) on its own endpoint and declares no dead-letter name. Retries and dead letters parks failed invoices on a queue of their own.

A job that fails leaves for a second queue the service binds, where park reads it under jobs.dead. Macros Manual examples/zmq_settlement_dead_letters.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let dead = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5561")).bindable(); let parked = dead.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled( "worker", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { // Every failed job leaves for the second queue, under the name it is read by. b.include(work).dead_letter("jobs.dead").out_retry(parked) }, ) .with_broker_labeled("dead", dead, |b| b.include(park)) } examples/manual/zmq_settlement_dead_letters.rs fn app() -> impl App { let dead = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5561")).bindable(); let parked = dead.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled( "worker", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { // Every failed job leaves for the second queue, under the name it is read by. b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) .dead_letter("jobs.dead") .out_retry(parked) }, ) .with_broker_labeled("dead", dead, |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs.dead", Park).build()) }) }

Where copies go follows the side: a bound subscription takes its own, and one that dials and every responder name a destination. out_retry(policy) sets the publisher the retry copies leave through. A ZmqQueue or ZmqFanout subscription that binds its endpoint is an address of its own. Its copies go back to that endpoint, so the mount names no destination, and .out_retry(Publish) states the default. A subscription that dials reads from a peer that only sends, so it has no address to send copies to. Its mount site names one with .out_retry(policy).to("name"). The policy is often a queue on another broker, which bindable() and .bind(Publish) turn into a publisher of this mount. On a dialing subscription, .out_retry(policy) without a destination does not compile, on a with_broker scope and on a Router alike. A mount that binds no retry slot is refused before the subscription opens, with an error naming the subscription. This holds for a mount that never asks for a retry too, because the runtime pairs the publisher either way. Every ZmqRpc responder names a destination too. A request has no address a copy could return to: answers travel to the identity of the peer that asked, and the reply publisher refuses a plain name. Retries and dead letters mounts both forms, a worker that binds and a worker that dials.

The worker dials a ventilator and sends its copies to a queue it binds itself, where the same handler takes them. The copies carry the count, so the cap of three holds across both subscriptions. Macros Manual examples/zmq_settlement_out_retry.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let retries = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5560")).bindable(); let copies = retries.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://ventilator:5555")), |b| { // The ventilator takes nothing back, so the copies go to the queue bound below. b.include(handle) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .out_retry(copies) .to("jobs") }, ) .with_broker(retries, |b| { // A bound queue takes its own copies back, so this mount names no destination. b.include(handle).max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) }) } examples/manual/zmq_settlement_out_retry.rs fn app() -> impl App { let retries = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5560")).bindable(); let copies = retries.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://ventilator:5555")), |b| { // The ventilator takes nothing back, so the copies go to the queue bound below. b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .out_retry(copies) .to("jobs") }, ) .with_broker(retries, |b| { // A bound queue takes its own copies back, so this mount names no destination. b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) }) }

retry_after(delay) publishes a copy after the delay, and max_attempts caps the copies through the framework's x-ruststream-retry-count header. The runtime waits out the delay and publishes a copy of the delivery, its payload and headers as they arrived. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER incremented, and a handler reads it like any other header. The copy waits in the memory of the service, so a process that stops before the delay is over loses it. max_attempts(n) caps the deliveries of one message at the mount site, the first one included. ZMTP has no delivery counter, so the framework counts through that header, and the cap holds wherever the copies travel. Under a cap a plain retry travels as a copy too. The delivery that reaches the cap goes to the dead-letter destination, and with none it is dropped with a warning naming the subscription. The copies leave through the Retry slot, which out_retry sets. On a queue the service binds, a copy goes back into the same queue. The copy carries the bytes of the delivery, so a codec named at the retry position encodes nothing. A .transform(..) there reads the delivery it retries, which is where a service marks a redelivery. Retries and dead letters retries a failed job into its own queue with a cap.

A job that fails gets five deliveries, 30 seconds apart, and each copy returns to the queue the worker binds. Macros Manual examples/zmq_retries.rs #[subscriber("jobs")] async fn handle(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { match run(job) { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "the job failed, retrying"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(30)) } } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { // Five deliveries at most, the first one included; the copies return to this queue. b.include(handle) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .out_retry(Publish) }, ) } examples/manual/zmq_retries.rs /// Works a job, and asks for another try in 30 seconds when it fails. struct Work; impl Handle<Job> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(run(job).map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "the job failed, retrying"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(30)) })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { // Five deliveries at most, the first one included; the copies return to this queue. b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .out_retry(Publish) }, ) }

A subscription is a name, and the name is frame 0 of every message; #[subscriber("jobs")] is the whole declaration. Every message travels as three frames, and the first one holds the name the publisher sent it under. That name is the whole declaration of a subscription, and the mount site carries every other setting. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, handler). Only ZmqFanout reads the name: it hands a subscription every message whose name starts with the subscription's, as Prefixes describes. A ZmqQueue or ZmqRpc subscription takes every message its socket receives, whatever frame 0 says. So a second kind of work takes an endpoint of its own. How many subscriptions a broker takes follows from the side. An endpoint this service binds is one socket, read by the subscription that bound it, and a second subscription there is refused when it opens. Subscriptions that dial are sockets of their own, so several of them dial one peer. Nothing is stored on the way. A subscription that attaches late has no backlog to read, a restart replays nothing, and .start_at(..) does not compile on these brokers.

A worker binds tcp://0.0.0.0:5555 and names its subscription jobs. A peer that pushes a message under another name to that endpoint reaches the same handler. Macros Manual examples/zmq_subscriptions_name.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; #[subscriber("jobs")] async fn work(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "working on the job"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| b.include(work), ) } examples/manual/zmq_subscriptions_name.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; struct Work; impl Handle<Job> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "working on the job"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()), ) }

A slice handler on a queue or fan-out gets a batch assembled on this side, closed at the size the mount names or 20 ms after its first delivery. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. A receive on a socket yields one multipart message, so a peer still sends one message at a time, in the same frames. The subscription collects the deliveries itself. A batch closes once it holds n deliveries, or 20 ms after its first one, whichever comes first. The 20 ms is a constant of the crate. So a busy socket fills batches to n, and a quiet one hands over batches of one, 20 ms after each message arrived. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch, and a Vec<HandlerOutcome> answers them one by one. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) settles the batch and Err(outcomes) settles it delivery by delivery. A ZmqRpc responder takes no batches, and .batch(..) on one does not compile. A responder answers each request at the peer that sent it, while a batch carries one publish context for all of its replies. The compile error names ZmqRpcSubscriber, which implements no BatchSubscriber. Pipelines with PUSH/PULL runs a sink that collects results in batches.

Three jobs pushed at once arrive in one call. A job pushed alone arrives 20 ms after it was pushed. Macros Manual examples/zmq_batches.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; /// Stores the jobs of one batch in a single round-trip. #[subscriber("jobs")] async fn drain(jobs: &[Job]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "stored a batch of jobs"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { // At most 32 jobs per call. b.include(drain.batch(nonzero!(32))) }, ) } examples/manual/zmq_batches.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; /// Stores the jobs of one batch in a single round-trip; `Ok` settles the whole batch. struct Drain; impl Handle<[Job]> for Drain { fn handle( &self, jobs: &[Job], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "stored a batch of jobs"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { // At most 32 jobs per call. b.include(subscriber("jobs", Drain).batch(nonzero!(32)).build()) }, ) }

On ZmqFanout a subscription named orders receives orders.created too: the name is a prefix filter, the protocol's own rule. A SUB socket subscribes with the subscription's name, and a message reaches it when frame 0 starts with that name. The comparison runs byte by byte and knows no separator. So orders takes orders.created and orders.shipped, and orders-archive as well. A name that ends with the separator, such as orders., takes the dotted family and leaves the lookalike out. A message that matches no subscription is dropped without an error. The rule is the same on both sides. A subscription that binds the fan-out and one that dials a publisher filter alike, and each subscription that dials is a socket with its own filter. A message this service publishes to its own bound fan-out is matched the same way, so a name under the subscription's prefix comes back to it. In the generated document, a fan-out publish channel reports nameFrame: the prefix a SUB peer subscribes with to receive it. Broadcast with PUB/SUB runs a watcher that subscribes to every job announcement by prefix.

The auditor reads every order event and leaves the archive records alone. Macros Manual examples/zmq_subscriptions_prefixes.rs use ruststream_zeromq::fanout::prelude::*; /// Every order event, `orders.created`, `orders.shipped`, and no `orders-archive` record. #[subscriber("orders.")] async fn audit(event: &OrderEvent) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.order_id, "order event audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("auditor", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5556")), |b| b.include(audit), ) } examples/manual/zmq_subscriptions_prefixes.rs use ruststream_zeromq::fanout::prelude::*; /// Every order event, `orders.created`, `orders.shipped`, and no `orders-archive` record. struct Audit; impl Handle<OrderEvent> for Audit { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.order_id, "order event audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("auditor", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5556")), |b| b.include(subscriber("orders.", Audit).build()), ) }

read_ahead bounds how many deliveries a subscription reads ahead of its handler, 1000 by default; past it the sender waits. A subscription reads its socket on a task of its own and hands the deliveries to its handler through a buffer. read_ahead sets the size of that buffer, counted in deliveries. When the buffer is full, the subscription stops reading. The socket buffers fill in turn, and the peer's send waits until the handler catches up. So a slow handler slows its sender down, and the memory of this process stays bounded. On PUB/SUB the waiting sender is the PUB socket, held back by its slowest matching subscriber, as Backpressure draws. The setting belongs to the broker: ZmqQueue::read_ahead, ZmqFanout::read_ahead and ZmqRpc::read_ahead take a NonZeroUsize. Every subscription mounted on the broker reads with that bound, and a clone of the broker keeps its own value. The in-process transport hands deliveries over without a bound, so a test sees the bound only over sockets, in a live test. Running in production sets the bound from the environment.

Each frame takes the renderer seconds, so it reads four frames ahead and leaves the rest with the sender. TestApp::start connects each ZeroMQ broker in process: the pattern's routing, the socket's refusals, and no settlement. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses a broker by its production type. tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>() names a queue this service binds, tb.broker::<ZmqQueue<Connect>>() one it dials, and tb.broker_named(..) a broker mounted under a label. The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode and turns on the core's harness with it. The in-process transport carries the frames a socket carries. A publish is framed as the socket publisher frames it, and a subscription reads the frames as its socket reads them. So a header value the text frame cannot hold is refused, and a request arrives stamped with the peer that sent it. A test's input arrives the way a peer in another process sends it. Which subscriptions a message reaches is the pattern's own rule: Queue: a subscription that binds takes whatever a peer pushes to its endpoint, and subscriptions that dial take a peer's messages in turn. Fan-out: every subscription whose name is a prefix of the message's name, on either side. Request and reply: a request reaches the responder, and its answer reaches the peer that asked and no subscription. A publish of this service reaches its own subscription only through the endpoint that subscription binds. On an endpoint the service dials, or binds with no subscription, the message leaves for a peer in another process: the test reads it with published, and no subscription receives it. The socket's refusals hold too: a publish a bound queue would hand back to its own subscription (Replies), any publish on an endpoint a subscription dials, a second subscription on a bound endpoint, an answer to a peer that is gone. Settlement is the socket's as well, so a handler that settles by a plain retry fails its test instead of losing its message in production. What only sockets show, such as the read-ahead bound or a port another process holds, is for a live test. Testing a ZeroMQ service tests a worker in process, with its delays on a paused clock.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-zeromq = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } The worker binds its queue and sends each result to a sink it dials. The test pushes a job and reads the result the worker published. Macros Manual examples/zmq_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_job_is_worked_and_its_result_published() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; // The job arrives the way a ventilator pushes it. tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>() .message(&Job { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>() .subscriber("jobs") .assert_called_once() .with(&Job { id: 7 }); tb.broker::<ZmqQueue<Connect>>() .published::<Done>("results") .assert_called_once() .with(&Done { id: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } examples/manual/zmq_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_job_is_worked_and_its_result_published() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; // The job arrives the way a ventilator pushes it. tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>() .message(&Job { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>() .subscriber("jobs") .assert_called_once() .with(&Job { id: 7 }); tb.broker::<ZmqQueue<Connect>>() .published::<Done>("results") .assert_called_once() .with(&Done { id: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) }

TestApp::start_live runs the same test over loopback sockets in every cargo test, for back-pressure and the real frames. It connects each broker through its ordinary connect, so every subscription binds or dials a real socket. ZeroMQ needs no server, so a live test needs no stand and no switch, and runs wherever cargo test runs. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A live test binds tcp://127.0.0.1:0: the system picks a free port, so tests that run in parallel never collide. An ipc:// path unique to the test serves the same purpose. A test's input leaves through the broker's own publisher, so on a bound queue it carries the subscription's own name. The fan-out's publisher reads its own subscription's filter before its first send, so a live fan-out test publishes once, as an in-process one does. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what reached it, ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process transport leaves out: the read-ahead bound and the back-pressure it puts on a sender, a port another process holds, and the frames a peer in another language sends. Testing a ZeroMQ service runs the same test in process and over sockets.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one over loopback sockets. In the default envelope every message is three frames, name, headers, payload, so a peer in any language composes one with send_multipart. ZeroMQ carries messages made of frames and leaves their meaning to the application. This crate gives every message on PUSH/PULL and PUB/SUB the same three frames: the name, the headers and the payload. The layout is the Frames envelope, which every broker reads and writes unless it names another; Envelopes shows the others. The name frame is the subscription's name on the fan-out, matched as a prefix; a queue takes every message whatever its name says. The header frame is text, and an empty frame means no headers. A message of two frames, a name and a payload, reads as a message without headers, so a minimal peer can skip the middle frame. A message of one frame is what a plain ZeroMQ peer sends: that frame is the payload, whole, the name is empty and there are no headers. On the fan-out a SUB matches its prefix against that same frame, so a plain PUB's message reaches a subscription whose name prefixes it, and the handler reads the frame as it was sent, prefix included. A message of more than three frames has no place for the frames past the payload, and it surfaces on the subscription as ZmqError::Wire, naming how many frames it had. The payload frame is what the service's codec wrote, so a peer agrees on the codec only: with the default JSON codec it is the document the handler's input type deserializes from. Bytes a service already holds encoded go out through a #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] newtype, and no codec runs on them. A name frame that is not UTF-8 surfaces on the subscription as ZmqError::Wire. On DEALER/ROUTER a request has the same three frames, and its answer travels behind the requester's identity, as Identity frame shows. Peers in other languages feeds, watches and asks a service from Python peers.

frame 0: name UTF-8; the fan-out's subscribers filter on it as a prefix frame 1: headers UTF-8 "name: value" lines separated by \n; may be empty frame 2: payload the codec's output A Python peer pushes a job into a worker with pyzmq: socket.send_multipart([b"jobs", b"content-type: application/json", b'{"id": 2}']) The worker reads the jobs a Python PUSH socket sends, and pushes each result to a sink that a Python PULL socket binds. The sink reads the three frames results, the header lines and the JSON document {"id":2}.
